content: 1. Kala-azar must be designated as a notifiable or reportable disease within the country. This ensures that all cases are systematically documented and monitored. 2. Health programs should establish mechanisms to receive reports of kala-azar cases from private healthcare providers in endemic areas. These cases must be included in the calculation of incidence rates to ensure accurate epidemiological data. 3. Cases should be reported based on their originating implementation unit to prevent double-counting. A unique Patient Identification Code should be introduced at every health facility, including those in the private sector, to streamline case tracking. 4. Active case-finding activities for kala-azar (KA) and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) should be conducted regularly, at least once a year, in each implementing unit (e.g., block, upazila, district). The specific strategy for active case finding should be tailored to the level of endemicity in the area. 5. A comprehensive information system must be established to collate data from all reporting units (block, upazila, district), including data from the private sector. This system should ensure that the incidence of kala-azar is reported as the number of cases per 10,000 population per year at the appropriate administrative level (e.g., upazila in Bangladesh, block in India, district in Nepal). 6. Surveillance data should be regularly analyzed, and appropriate feedback mechanisms should be implemented to provide consistent updates to reporting units. If the reported incidence rate in each implementing unit remains below 1 case per 10,000 population for at least three consecutive years, the country may initiate the process of validation for elimination. 7. Countries preparing to validate the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem may seek technical assistance from the World Health Organization (WHO) to compile a comprehensive report. This report should include documentation of preconditions met, historical and epidemiological data, elimination program strategies, surveillance systems, and robust estimates of unreported cases. 8. The report should also detail diagnostic and treatment strategies, quality control measures, and annual data on endemic units, population at risk, incidence rates of KA and PKDL, active case-finding activities, and the proportion of private health facilities reporting cases. 9. An independent validation team (IVT), constituted by WHO, will evaluate the reliability of the country’s report. The team will include experts in relevant fields such as epidemiology and entomology, ensuring no conflicts of interest. 10. The IVT will spend 2–3 weeks in the country, reviewing the national program, visiting endemic sites, interviewing health personnel, and examining records at central and peripheral levels. The team will independently assess areas with poor documentation or unusual transmission risks. 11. The IVT will present its findings to the national program and WHO, concluding whether elimination has been achieved or not. The report will outline the reasons for their decision. 12. Once elimination is verified, monitoring the sustainability of elimination will involve annual country reports and joint monitoring missions (national and international experts) every three years. 13. Active case detection (ACD) methods validated for kala-azar and PKDL include the blanket approach, camp approach, index case-based approach, and incentive-based approach. Each method has specific applications based on the endemicity level and resource availability. 14. The blanket approach involves house-to-house visits by trained health workers in endemic areas and is considered the gold standard but is costly and recommended only during outbreaks. 15. The camp approach organizes health camps in endemic communities, where mobile teams screen for KA and PKDL. This method is sensitive and effective in high-endemic areas. 16. The index case-based approach focuses on identifying new cases among household members and neighbors of recently diagnosed cases. It is preferred in moderate-to-low endemic areas. 17. The incentive-based approach rewards health workers for detecting new cases. This method is useful in low-endemic areas but requires strict supervision to prevent misuse of funds. 18. Passive case detection (PCD) relies on self-reported cases in public and private health facilities. While integrated into existing health systems, it may be expensive for patients seeking multiple diagnoses before confirmation. 19. The frequency of ACD depends on the method used. The camp approach is effective when conducted twice a year, while the index case and incentive-based approaches should be ongoing throughout the year. The blanket approach is reserved for outbreak situations. 20. Cost estimates for ACD methods range from approximately $20 to $600 per new case detected. The blanket approach is the most expensive, followed by the incentive, camp, and index approaches. 21. The index case-based approach involves systematic procedures for identifying and referring chronic fever cases and skin lesion cases in low-endemic areas. It requires trained health workers, proper documentation, and a defined reporting system. 22. Preparatory activities for the index case-based approach include identifying target areas, training health workers, and establishing supervision and monitoring plans. Monthly reviews of reported cases and house-to-house searches around index cases are essential components. 23. The validation process for kala-azar elimination involves thorough documentation, independent evaluation, and ongoing monitoring to ensure sustained elimination as a public health problem.
